title: Dionysus: the god of wine and excess
subtitle: Wine, theater, transgression
subject: mythologie
description: God of wine and ecstasy, Dionysus is also the patron of Greek theater. Born twice, he erases the border between order and chaos.

hero.hook: The god of wine does not only bring drunkenness: he also invents theater.

blocks.text: **Dionysus** is the most paradoxical of the Greek gods. God of wine, of the vine and of drunkenness, he is above all the god of transformation. Unlike the Olympians fixed on their mountaintop, he wanders, followed by a noisy procession.
He erases the borders between divine and human, order and chaos, life and death. Out of his festivals came [[Theatre]], one of the greatest legacies of Greece.

sections.title: Born twice: from Semele to the thigh of Zeus

blocks.text: Dionysus is born out of a tragedy. **Zeus**, king of the gods, loves the mortal [[Semele]], a princess of Thebes. **Hera**, Zeus's jealous wife, pushes her to ask her lover to show himself in his true divine form.

blocks.caption: Dionysus, god of wine, ecstasy and transformation

blocks.text: Zeus obeys. His lightning kills Semele. To save the child, Zeus sews him into his own thigh until birth. Dionysus is therefore “twice born,” and that is the origin of the song dedicated to him: the [[Dithyramb]].
This myth explains why Dionysus is both mortal and divine: he has a human mother and an Olympian father who “carried” him.

As an adult, Dionysus travels the world to spread his cult. His followers, mostly women called **Maenads** or Bacchae, leave the city for the mountains. There, dance, music and wine bring on a trance: being “possessed by the god.”
These rites, called [[mysteries]], turn the social order upside down. For one night, reason gives way. The god promises release, but also madness for anyone who rejects him.

blocks.caption: Bacchae in trance: the cult that overturns the order of the city

blocks.text: One day pirates capture Dionysus to sell him. He turns the oars into snakes and makes a vine grow up the mast. Terrified, the men jump into the sea and become dolphins.

sections.title: Out of chaos, theater is born

blocks.text: In Athens, this god of excess became the patron of a civic art: theater. In the 6th century BC, the **Great Dionysia** staged drama contests. Everything started from the dithyramb, the choral song sung in the god's honor.

blocks.caption: The Great Dionysia: worship becomes civic spectacle

blocks.text: When one singer stepped out of the chorus to answer it, the actor was born. Tragedy became a place where the city could look at its fears and its conflicts without falling into real chaos. That is [[catharsis]]: purging emotions by watching them.

events.title: A double birth
events.detail: Semele dies; Zeus finishes the pregnancy.

events.title: Rites of the Maenads
events.detail: Ecstasy, wine, the social order turned upside down.

blocks.text: In the 19th century, the philosopher **Nietzsche** set two forces against each other: [[Apollo]], god of measure and clarity, and Dionysus, the force of drunkenness and creative chaos. For him, that tension, the [[Apollonian and Dionysian (Nietzsche)]], explains the greatness of Greek tragedy.
Dionysus remains the god who reminds us of a simple truth: without a little disorder, there is no art, no festival and no invention.
**Dionysus**, born twice, god of wine and ecstasy, inspired the rites that gave birth to Greek **theater**. He embodies the fertile tension between measure and excess.
